blocks.text: The learning rate is the single multiplier in the gradient descent update rule that controls how large each step is, and getting it wrong is one of the single most common reasons a model fails to train well. Too large and training diverges, too small and training crawls, making the learning rate one of the most important hyperparameters to tune correctly.

1. What the Learning Rate Controls

In the gradient descent update rule, parameter minus learning rate times gradient, the learning rate scales how far each step moves along the gradient direction. It does not change the direction of the step, only its size.

code.content:
import numpy as np
gradient = np.array([2.0])
for lr in [0.001, 0.1, 1.0]:
    step_size = lr * gradient
    print(lr, step_size)

blocks.text: Every gradient based optimizer, no matter how sophisticated, ultimately relies on some version of this same scaling idea, making the learning rate one of the most universally important hyperparameters across all of machine learning.
Some frameworks call this quantity step size instead of learning rate, especially in optimization literature outside of deep learning specifically, both terms refer to exactly the same multiplier.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A gradient of 4 with a learning rate of 0.1 produces a step of 0.4, while the same gradient with a learning rate of 0.01 produces a step of only 0.04, ten times smaller for the exact same underlying gradient.

blocks.text: 2. Too High a Learning Rate: Divergence

A learning rate that is too large causes each step to overshoot the minimum, sometimes landing further away than the starting point, and the loss can oscillate wildly or even grow without bound instead of decreasing.

code.content:
def gradient_descent_1d(start, learning_rate, steps, grad_fn):
    x = start
    history = [x]
    for _ in range(steps):
        x = x - learning_rate * grad_fn(x)
        history.append(x)
    return history

print(gradient_descent_1d(5.0, 1.5, 5, lambda x: 2*x))   # diverges, growing in magnitude

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Starting at 5.0 with a learning rate of 1.5 on the function 2x, the first step alone jumps to negative 10, already further from 0 than the starting point, and subsequent steps grow even larger in magnitude, a clear divergence pattern.

blocks.text: This kind of divergence is often visible almost immediately in a training log, the reported loss shooting up to extremely large numbers or turning into NaN within the first few steps.
Recovering from divergence usually requires restarting training from an earlier saved checkpoint with a smaller learning rate, rather than continuing forward from the diverged state.
3. Too Low a Learning Rate: Slow Convergence

A learning rate that is too small takes tiny, cautious steps, and while it will eventually approach the minimum, it can require an impractically large number of steps to get there, wasting significant training time.

code.content: print(gradient_descent_1d(5.0, 0.001, 5, lambda x: 2*x))   # barely moves after 5 steps

blocks.text: In a real training run, an excessively small learning rate can make the difference between a model finishing training in hours versus never meaningfully improving within any practical time budget.
A telltale sign of too small a learning rate is a loss curve that decreases, but so gradually that after many epochs it still looks nearly flat.
Increasing the learning rate is usually the first, cheapest fix to try when training progress looks unreasonably slow, before investigating more complex explanations.
4. A Well Tuned Learning Rate
A well chosen learning rate takes steps large enough to make meaningful progress each iteration, without overshooting so far that the loss starts oscillating or diverging.

blocks.alt: Loss curves under different learning rates
blocks.caption: A well tuned rate descends steadily without oscillating or crawling

blocks.text: Visualizing the loss curve over training steps, as this diagram illustrates conceptually, is one of the fastest ways to diagnose whether a chosen learning rate is too high, too low, or roughly appropriate.
There is rarely a single perfect learning rate, a reasonably wide range of values around the ideal one will still train successfully, just with somewhat different speed and final performance.
This visual comparison is worth revisiting any time a new model or dataset is trained for the first time, since the ideal rate genuinely differs across different problems.
Reaching this well tuned regime is rarely a matter of luck, it typically comes from a combination of the range test technique and iterative experimentation on the specific problem at hand.
5. Learning Rate Decay

A learning rate schedule reduces the learning rate over the course of training, starting with larger steps to make fast early progress, then shrinking the steps later on to fine tune more precisely near a minimum.
Common decay schedules include step decay, dropping the rate by a fixed factor every few epochs, and cosine decay, smoothly reducing it following a cosine curve down to a small final value.
Reducing the learning rate late in training lets the optimizer fine tune its position near a minimum without the risk of overshooting it the way a larger, earlier rate might.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Using step decay with an initial rate of 0.1 that halves every 10 epochs, the rate becomes 0.05 at epoch 10, 0.025 at epoch 20, and so on, giving progressively finer adjustments as training continues.

blocks.text: 6. Learning Rate Warmup

Warmup starts training with a small learning rate and gradually increases it over the first several steps or epochs, before switching to the main decay schedule, helping avoid instability while model weights are still far from a reasonable region early in training.
A short warmup phase of just a few hundred steps is often enough to stabilize training, after which the main decay schedule takes over for the remainder of the run.
Warmup and decay are frequently combined into a single schedule, ramping the learning rate up briefly at the very start before letting it decay steadily for the remainder of training.
Skipping warmup on a large, complex model can occasionally cause training to fail entirely within the first few steps, making it a cheap, low risk safeguard worth including by default.
7. Adaptive Learning Rates

Optimizers like Adam and RMSprop adjust the effective learning rate separately for every individual parameter, based on the recent history of gradients for that parameter, rather than using one single fixed rate for the entire model.

code.content:
import torch
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001)   # Adam adapts the effective rate per parameter internally

blocks.text: These per-parameter adjustments are especially useful when different parameters naturally need very different effective step sizes, a common situation in deep networks with many layers of varying scale.
Despite this per-parameter adaptivity, an overall base learning rate still needs to be chosen for adaptive optimizers, they reduce, but do not eliminate, the need for tuning.

Adam in particular has become an extremely common default optimizer choice specifically because it tends to work reasonably well across a wide range of problems without extensive learning rate tuning.
8. Finding a Good Learning Rate

A common practical technique, called a learning rate range test, trains for a short number of steps while gradually increasing the learning rate from very small to very large, plotting the loss against the rate to visually spot the largest rate that still steadily decreases the loss.

The point where the loss starts increasing sharply during this range test marks roughly where the learning rate becomes too large, and a value somewhat below that point is typically chosen as the actual training rate.
This range test is typically run for only a few hundred steps, far short of a full training run, specifically to keep the search itself cheap.
Some libraries automate this entire range test procedure, plotting the resulting loss curve directly and suggesting a reasonable starting learning rate without any manual tuning.
9. Learning Rate and Batch Size

The stochastic gradient descent lesson noted that larger batch sizes produce less noisy gradient estimates, which generally tolerate a proportionally larger learning rate, a relationship worth tuning together rather than independently.

A widely used, though only approximate, rule of thumb scales the learning rate linearly with batch size, doubling the batch size roughly doubling the learning rate as a reasonable starting point for further tuning.

Ignoring this relationship, changing batch size without revisiting the learning rate, is a common, easy to overlook source of a training run performing worse than an earlier one that used a different batch size.
This interaction is one of several reasons changing a single hyperparameter in isolation, without considering related ones, so often produces confusing or disappointing results.
10. A Worked Example
Run gradient descent on the function f(x) = x squared starting at x = 10, comparing learning rates of 0.01, 0.5, and 1.1 over 10 steps.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Learning rate","Behavior"],"rows":[["0.01","converges very slowly, still far from 0 after 10 steps"],["0.5","converges cleanly to near 0"],["1.1","diverges, growing in magnitude each step"]]}

blocks.text: This single experiment concretely demonstrates all three learning rate regimes, slow crawling, clean convergence, and outright divergence, on the exact same starting point and function.

Rerunning this same experiment with a different starting point, such as x = 3 instead of x = 10, would show the same three qualitative behaviors, confirming the pattern depends on the learning rate itself rather than the specific starting position.

Simple, hand-computable examples like this one are worth returning to whenever a new optimizer or learning rate schedule needs to be understood before applying it to a much larger, harder to inspect model.
11. Common Mistakes

items: Using the same fixed learning rate throughout all of training without considering a decay schedule, especially on longer training runs.
Assuming a diverging loss is a bug in the model architecture, when an overly large learning rate is a far more common culprit.
Copying a learning rate from a different paper or project without adjusting for a different batch size, optimizer, or dataset.
Tuning the learning rate in isolation without considering how it interacts with batch size and the choice of optimizer.

blocks.text: A related trap worth naming directly: increasing the learning rate to fix slow training without first checking whether the real bottleneck is something else entirely, such as a poorly scaled input feature or an unsuitable model architecture.
Another subtle trap: assuming a learning rate that works well for one model architecture will transfer directly to a very different one without any retuning.
It is also easy to forget that a learning rate tuned for one loss function may not transfer well to a different loss function, even on the exact same model and data.
12. Practice: Tune a Learning Rate
Try several learning rates on a simple quadratic function and identify the largest one that still converges without oscillating.
Narrowing in on the boundary between convergence and divergence this way builds direct, hands on intuition for the tradeoff at the center of this entire lesson.
Once the boundary is found, try a rate just below it and just above it, and compare how each behaves over a longer run of 30 or more steps.
This kind of hands-on boundary search is a transferable skill, the exact same experimental process applies just as well to tuning a real model as it does to this simple quadratic example.
Key Takeaway

The learning rate scales how large each gradient descent step is, and choosing it well requires balancing speed of convergence against the risk of overshooting or diverging. Schedules like decay and warmup, along with adaptive optimizers, exist specifically to manage this tradeoff more gracefully than a single fixed rate can.

The local minima and global minima lessons immediately ahead cover what gradient descent is actually searching for, and how the learning rate choice interacts with the shape of the loss surface it navigates.
A learning rate range test, covered in section 8, remains one of the fastest, most practical ways to get a reasonable starting value before investing in a full hyperparameter search.

Every optimizer variant covered across this module, plain gradient descent, stochastic and mini-batch versions, and adaptive methods, all still depend fundamentally on getting this one number in a reasonable range.
A single well chosen learning rate, or a well designed schedule, is often the difference between a model that trains successfully within a reasonable budget and one that never converges at all.
